contraindications: TOXIC: Calotropis gigantea/procera contains cardiac glycosides (calotropin, calatoxin, uscharin) with digitalis-like action; unsupervised ingestion can cause vomiting, burning GI pain, arrhythmia and heart block.
Do NOT swallow the latex or self-prepared plant parts - only classically processed (shodhit) formulations under qualified supervision are ever used.

Pregnancy: strictly avoid - traditional use as an abortifacient; latex/toxicity risk.
interactions: Digoxin and other cardiac glycosides / antiarrhythmics - additive digitalis-like activity increases toxicity risk.

contraindications: Species note: Charaka's kataka is Strychnos potatorum (clearing nut, nirmali) - NOT the poisonous strychnine tree (Strychnos nux-vomica, kupeelu); do not substitute.

The seed alkaloid fraction is neuroactive in animals when injected (restlessness, tremors, convulsions, hypotension) - keep to traditional small oral doses; never use alkaloid/injectable preparations.
Pregnancy: no pregnancy-specific safety data - use only in traditional small food/dose amounts.
interactions: No clinically documented drug interactions; contains strychnine-family alkaloids in trace amounts (diaboline major) - keep doses traditional.

dosha_caution: Bitter, light - Tiktaka (bitter) group; traditionally regarded as cooling and diuretic.

contraindications: Hypothyroidism: holy basil might lower thyroxine levels; in theory this could worsen hypothyroidism (WebMD).
Surgery: holy basil might slow blood clotting, increasing bleeding risk during and after surgery; stop using at least 2 weeks before a scheduled surgery (WebMD).
Avoid prolonged chewing of the raw leaves in large quantities for extended periods - the astringent leaves can damage tooth enamel over time (MedicineNet).
interactions: Medications for diabetes - holy basil might lower blood sugar; taking it with diabetes medications might cause blood sugar to drop too low (WebMD).
Medications that slow blood clotting (anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs) - holy basil might slow clotting and increase bruising/bleeding risk (WebMD).
Pentobarbital (Nembutal) - taking holy basil seed oil with pentobarbital might cause too much drowsiness (WebMD).
pregnancy_flag: Avoid - possibly unsafe during pregnancy or when trying to become pregnant; in animals large doses seem to reduce the chance of pregnancy or a full-length pregnancy (WebMD). Breast-feeding: insufficient data, avoid use.
dosha_caution: Light, pungent and heating - generally tridoshic as a food spice; used for kapha/vata respiratory conditions in classical practice

contraindications: Pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid moringa (MSK; corroborated by Drugs.com 'Avoid use' - pregnancy/lactation safety data lacking).
Moringa root and root extracts are possibly unsafe when taken by mouth - the roots contain spirochin, a toxic substance (RxList).

Reported rare serious adverse events after consuming moringa leaf/powder: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, cutaneous toxicity with respiratory distress and tongue edema, and anaphylaxis - case reports (MSK, Drugs.com).
interactions: Cytochrome P450 substrates including CYP3A4 - moringa increased rifampin bioavailability and inhibited CYP3A4 in preclinical models; clinical relevance not yet determined (MSK). Also notes impaired clearance of CYP3A4/CYP1A2 and P-gp substrates and increased nevirapine concentrations (Drugs.com, WebMD).
Sitagliptin - chronic co-administration decreased the antihyperglycemic effect in an animal model; clinical relevance not yet determined (MSK).
Medications for diabetes - moringa might lower blood sugar; monitor blood sugar closely (WebMD).

Levothyroxine - potential interaction: animal studies suggest moringa inhibits thyroxine-to-triiodothyronine conversion, and RxList suggests it may decrease levothyroxine absorption; framed as potential, not confirmed (Drugs.com, RxList).
pregnancy_flag: Avoid - pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid use (MSK); no pregnancy/lactation safety data; abortifacient effects reported with oral leaf extract in rats (Drugs.com).
dosha_caution: Bitter, pungent and heating - shigru is classically tikshna/ushna and used for kapha conditions; not used as a daily teal in large amounts in classical practice
